```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
Sys.setenv(TZ = "UTC")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
data_dir <- normalizePath(file.path(dirname(knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE)),
                                    "../../dev/article-data/space-time-plot-sampling"))
knitr::read_chunk(file.path(data_dir, "generate_population.R"))
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = data_dir)
```

Forest inventories often revisit only part of their plots in a given year.
We extend the [spatial model](spatial-effects-plot-sampling.html) so nearby
plots can share information both across space and across measurement years.
The magnitude effect and the species factor now vary with location and time.
We estimate their covariance parameters, map combined intercepts, and compare
forest species-by-DBH densities at the beginning and end of the study.

The example starts with all 151 plots in year 0 and revisits 25 plots in each
of years 1 through 9, giving 376 plot measurements. It uses the same forest
geometry and LiDAR canopy heights as the [data article](plot-sampling-data.html)
[@spitta2026lidar]. Counts are simulated. Canopy height is held constant over
time so changes in this example arise through the space-time effects.

::: {.alert .alert-info role="note"}
**Example data**

[Download the space-time data (ZIP)](downloads/space-time-plot-sampling.zip){.btn .btn-primary download="space-time-plot-sampling.zip"}

Extract the archive and use the folder containing `data/` as your R working
directory. It includes the generated counts, known effects, forest polygons,
and `generate_population.R`. Reading these files avoids generating the full
GP population again; the optional generator uses seed 1.
:::

## Read the repeated measurements

`site_id` identifies a physical location. `plot_id` identifies a measurement
at a particular site and year, so repeated measurements have different
`plot_id` values. The prediction file contains the 4,812 forest cells in
years 0 and 9. `location_id` links each prediction to its cell polygon.

```{r}
#| label: read-data
library(magComp)
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)

plots <- read_csv("data/plots.csv")

prediction <- read_csv("data/prediction.csv")

true_parameters <- read_csv("data/true_parameters.csv", na = "NA")

forest <- st_read("data/forest.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)

prediction_cells <- st_read("data/prediction_cells.gpkg", quiet = TRUE) |>
  rename(location_id = plot_id)

plots |> count(year, name = "Measured plots") |> knitr::kable()
```

We map the measurements to see how the inventory covers the forest over time.

```{r}
#| label: fig-visit-locations
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Sampled locations in each year. The initial inventory measures every plot; later years remeasure subsets."
plot_locations <- plots |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("easting", "northing"), crs = st_crs(forest), remove = FALSE)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = forest, fill = "grey95", color = "grey70", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = plot_locations, color = "#0072B2", size = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ year, ncol = 5) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void()
```

## Describe the space-time model

The magnitude model retains the same regression and negative-binomial count
likelihood, with a space-time effect in the log density,

$$
\log M_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+v(\mathbf{s}_i,t_i),\qquad
N_i\mid M_i,r_M\sim\operatorname{NB}(a_i M_i,r_M).
$$

Here $x_i$ is standardized canopy height, $a_i$ is area in hectares, and
$t_i$ is measurement year. The separable exponential covariance is

$$
\operatorname{Cov}\{v(\mathbf{s},t),v(\mathbf{s}',t')\}
=\sigma_v^2\exp\{-\phi_v\|\mathbf{s}-\mathbf{s}'\|
                 -\lambda_v|t-t'|\}.
$$

The spatial decay $\phi_v$ governs dependence with distance, and the temporal
decay $\lambda_v$ governs dependence with elapsed time. Larger values give
faster decreases in correlation. At a fixed site, latent effects a year apart
have correlation $\exp(-\lambda_v)$. At a fixed year, the model reduces
to the exponential spatial covariance used in the
[spatial-effects article](spatial-effects-plot-sampling.html).

Species allocation uses an independent, unit-variance space-time factor,

$$
\pi_{ij}=\Phi\{\alpha_{0j}+\alpha_{1j}x_i+
                       \lambda_j w(\mathbf{s}_i,t_i)\},
$$

with correlation $\exp\{-\phi_w\|\mathbf{s}-\mathbf{s}'\|
-\lambda_w|t-t'|\}$. The loadings $\lambda_j$ describe species responses to
this common factor; $\lambda_w$ is its temporal decay. Pine is the positive
anchor, oak has its own loading, and birch receives the remaining trees.
DBH allocation within species uses the same canopy-height regressions as
the full-model article, without additional random effects.

We generate the magnitude field with $\sigma_v=0.5$, $\phi_v=3$, and
$\lambda_v=0.35$, and the species field with $\phi_w=5$ and $\lambda_w=0.25$.
Spatial distances are in kilometers and time differences are in years.
Magnitude coefficients are $\beta_0=\log(350)$ and $\beta_1=-0.2$;
size is $r_M=1000$. Pine and oak loadings are 0.7 and -0.5.

Separability lets us generate the full GP with a spatial Cholesky factor

values, $L_S Z L_T^\mathsf{T}$ has the required covariance across sites and

## Fit the model

We arrange the counts into one row per measurement, species, and DBH class.
Time belongs to the measurement, so every category row for a given
`plot_id` has the same year and coordinates.

```{r}
#| label: model-data
species_order <- c("pine", "oak", "birch")
dbh_classes <- c("10-20", "20-30", "30-40", "40-50", "50+")

trees <- plots |>
  select(plot_id, area, x, easting_km, northing_km, year, contains(":")) |>
  pivot_longer(contains(":"), names_to = c("species", "dbh_class"),
               names_sep = ":", values_to = "count") |>
  mutate(species = factor(species, levels = species_order),
         dbh_class = ordered(dbh_class, levels = dbh_classes))

dat <- magCompData(trees, unit = plot_id, categories = c(species, dbh_class),
  tree_count = count, ordered = c(species = FALSE, dbh_class = TRUE),
  design = fixedArea(area))
```

The final coordinate in a space-time term is time. `cov_model = "sep_exp"`
selects the separable exponential correlation. We use 15 neighbors and set
`st_scale = 0.25`, making a one-year gap equivalent to 0.25 km when selecting
neighbors. This search scale stays fixed; the covariance uses the actual
spatial and temporal differences and estimates their separate decays.

The package supplies automatic priors and starting values. Here we explicitly
set uniform supports for the decays to show how to specify them. The same
supports apply to the magnitude field and the species factor, whose parameter
values are estimated separately.

```{r}
#| label: fit
covariance_prior <- list(phi = uniform(0.3, 10), lambda = uniform(0.05, 1))

fit <- magComp(
  dat,
  magnitude = ~ x + nngp(easting_km, northing_km, year, cov_model = "sep_exp",
                          st_scale = 0.25, m = 15, name = "space_time"),
  composition = magCompComposition(
    species ~ x + factor_nngp(easting_km, northing_km, year,
      cov_model = "sep_exp", st_scale = 0.25, m = 15,
      anchors = "pine", name = "space_time"),
    dbh_class | species ~ x
  ),
  priors = magCompPriors(
    magnitude = list(terms = list(space_time = list(covariance = covariance_prior))),
    composition = list(blocks = list(species = list(
      terms = list(space_time = list(covariance = covariance_prior)))))
  ),
  control = magCompControl(n_samples = 8000, n_burn = 3000, n_chains = 3,
    n_cores = 3, chain_seeds = 1:3, nb_size = 1000, verbose = FALSE)
)
```

Each chain retains 5,000 draws. Size remains fixed because the magnitude model
includes a random effect. `magCompCovModels()` lists the other available
covariance families. `magCompSettings(fit)` reports resolved priors, starting
values, and tuning. A covariance parameter can be held fixed with
`fixed(value)` in its corresponding starting entry.

## Examine parameters and combined intercepts

We compare the magnitude and species parameter estimates with their known
values. The temporal decays appear as `lambda_v` and `lambda_w[pine]`;
the loading rows have `parameter = "loadings"`.

```{r}
#| label: parameter-summary
parameter_summary <- summary(fit)

parameter_comparison <- parameter_summary |>
  filter(component == "magnitude" | block == "species") |>
  left_join(true_parameters, by = c("component", "block", "parameter", "index"))

parameter_comparison |>
  select(symbol, truth, mean, q2_5, q97_5, rhat, ess) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
    col.names = c("Parameter", "Truth", "Mean", "2.5%", "97.5%", "R-hat", "ESS"))
```

The intervals for both spatial and temporal decays include their generating
values, as do those for the magnitude variance and species loadings. The
magnitude intercept has a larger R-hat, about 1.06. Intercepts and latent effects
can trade off while leaving their sums nearly unchanged. As in the spatial
article, we also inspect the combined intercepts, averaged over the measured
plot visits within each posterior draw.

```{r}
#| label: combined-diagnostics
summary(fit, type = "combined", group = ".all") |>
  select(component, stick, mean, rhat, ess) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The combined-intercept R-hats are close to one, with much larger effective
sample sizes than the separate intercepts. These diagnostics concern the
combined coefficients. They do not replace
checking the separate covariance and loading parameters in the preceding table.

## Predict the forest in two years

We supply all cells in both years in one prediction call, retaining their
joint space-time dependence. The observation target draws new counts and
allocations in addition to new latent effects. We use 50 draws per chain for
the figures and summaries, while keeping every fitting draw for diagnostics.

```{r}
#| label: predict
set.seed(1)

predictions <- predict(
  fit,
  prediction |> select(plot_id, area, x, easting_km, northing_km, year),
  type = "density", target = "observation", summary = "samples",
  n_draws = 50, keep_effects = TRUE
)
```

### Map true and estimated relationships

The maps compare combined intercepts at the first and last years. Each
magnitude intercept is log density at average canopy height; the species
intercepts are on the probit scale. The maps use the same latent draws as
the density predictions.

```{r}
#| label: map-values
intercept_summary <- summary(samples(predictions, type = "combined")) |>
  mutate(plot_id = as.integer(unit),
         component = if_else(component == "magnitude", "Magnitude", str_to_title(stick)))

true_intercepts <- prediction |>
  select(plot_id, location_id, year, magnitude_intercept, pine_intercept, oak_intercept) |>
  pivot_longer(ends_with("intercept"), names_to = "component", values_to = "truth") |>
  mutate(component = recode(component, magnitude_intercept = "Magnitude",
                             pine_intercept = "Pine", oak_intercept = "Oak"))

map_values <- intercept_summary |>
  select(plot_id, component, Estimate = mean) |>
  left_join(true_intercepts, by = c("plot_id", "component")) |>
  rename(Truth = truth) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Truth, Estimate), names_to = "source", values_to = "intercept") |>
  mutate(source = factor(source, levels = c("Truth", "Estimate")))

intercept_maps <- prediction_cells |>
  left_join(map_values, by = "location_id", relationship = "many-to-many")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-magnitude-intercepts
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "True and estimated combined magnitude intercepts in years 0 and 9, on a common log-density scale."
ggplot(filter(intercept_maps, component == "Magnitude")) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = intercept), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = forest, fill = NA, color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.15) +
  facet_grid(year ~ source) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Combined\nintercept") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-species-intercepts
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-cap: "True and estimated combined species intercepts by year, on a common probit scale. Oak allocation is conditional on a tree not being pine."
ggplot(filter(intercept_maps, component != "Magnitude")) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = intercept), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = forest, fill = NA, color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.15) +
  facet_grid(component + year ~ source) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Combined\nintercept") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void()
```

### Summarize each year's forest distribution

We pass `year` as the grouping variable to `standSummary()`. Each year gets
its own area-weighted density, using the same forest cells. Omitting this
group would average across both years, which is a different target.

```{r}
#| label: forest-summary
forest_predictions <- standSummary(
  predictions, data = prediction, unit = plot_id, group = year,
  represented_area = area, summary = "samples"
)

forest_truth <- prediction |>
  select(year, area, contains(":")) |>
  pivot_longer(contains(":"), names_to = "category", values_to = "count") |>
  group_by(year, category) |>
  summarise(truth = sum(count) / sum(area), .groups = "drop")

forest_comparison <- summary(forest_predictions) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(unit)) |>
  left_join(forest_truth, by = c("year", "category")) |>
  separate_wider_delim(category, delim = ":", names = c("species", "dbh_class")) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species, levels = species_order),
         dbh_class = ordered(dbh_class, levels = dbh_classes))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest-distributions
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Forest species-by-DBH densities in years 0 and 9. Blue points and bars show posterior predictive means and 95% intervals; black horizontal marks show simulated truth."
ggplot(forest_comparison, aes(dbh_class, mean)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), width = 0.15, color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(aes(shape = "Estimate"), color = "#0072B2", size = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = truth, shape = "Truth"), size = 5) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Truth" = 95, "Estimate" = 16),
                     breaks = c("Truth", "Estimate"), name = NULL) +
  facet_grid(year ~ species) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "DBH class (cm)", y = "Trees per hectare") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The year-9 intervals are generally wider: only 25 plots were measured in
that year, and measurements from other years supply partial information
through temporal dependence.

These distributions combine canopy height with the estimated space-time
variation in abundance and species allocation. The model describes changing
distributions; it does not track individual trees or impose a growth model.
With time-varying canopy heights or other covariates, supply their values at
each observed and prediction date. Stand summaries can use the same draws,
with a grouping column that identifies each stand and year and the cell's
intersection area within that stand.
